title: The 'Hidden Tax': How a Weakening Dollar Is Squeezing American Consumers
summary: A silent force is eroding your purchasing power: the U.S. dollar has weakened significantly since President Trump's inauguration. The Dollar Index, which measures the greenback against major currencies, logged its steepest six-month decline in more than half a century. Though the slide has leveled off, the dollar remains about 10% lower than when Trump took office. Economists call it a "hidden tax." "What your dollar is going to be able to buy is going to shrink," said Thomas Savidge of the American Institute for Economic Research. A weaker currency makes imports more expensive — from French wine to Chinese electronics — and jacks up the cost of foreign travel. Your dollar now buys 16% fewer pesos in Mexico, and similar declines hit the Euro, Swiss franc, and others. Trump has openly cheered a weaker dollar, arguing it boosts American exports by making U.S. goods cheaper abroad. Corporate earnings calls reflect that: executives from Philip Morris to Coca-Cola have celebrated "favorable currency impacts." InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf called it "not unhelpful" for profits. But for the vast majority of U.S. businesses that don't export, the pain is real. David Navazio, CEO of medical supplier Gentell, operates plants in five countries. In each, the dollar's drop has increased his costs, forcing price hikes on bandages and other products. "A year ago, none of these were concerns," he said. "And it always hurts the consumer." The weak dollar adds another layer of cost pressures on top of tariffs and fuel spikes. For American families, the effect is most tangible at the grocery store, the gas pump, and the airport currency exchange. While a cheaper dollar might eventually help rebalance trade, for now, it's quietly taxing your wallet.
why_it_matters: A weak dollar doesn't just affect international trade — it reshapes the cost of everyday life, from the price of your favorite imported snack to what a family pays for a vacation abroad. Understanding exchange rates helps you see how global money moves can land right in your own pocket, influencing job opportunities and the affordability of the future you'll step into.

background_read: The U.S. Dollar Index was introduced in 1973 and is set at a base value of 100. It compares the dollar to six major currencies, including the euro, Japanese yen, and British pound. Its decline since Trump's inauguration is the steepest six-month drop since the early 1970s, when the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates collapsed.

A weaker dollar isn't all bad — it can help American manufacturers and farmers sell goods overseas because their products become cheaper for foreign buyers. But for U.S. consumers, it acts like a quiet tax. The article points out that your dollar now buys 16% fewer pesos in Mexico, and similar drops affect the euro and Swiss franc.

President Trump has long argued that a strong dollar punishes U.S. workers. In past administrations, Treasury secretaries typically maintained a 'strong dollar policy.' Trump's open cheerleading for a weaker currency breaks with that tradition. Tariffs on imports, which Trump also embraces, add to the price pressures that hit families at the grocery store and gas pump.

David Navazio is the CEO of Gentell, a medical supply company that operates plants in five countries. The weaker dollar has increased his production costs, forcing him to raise prices on items like bandages. His company's experience illustrates how currency swings ripple from executive offices all the way to a family's medicine cabinet.

perspectives.description: Companies that sell goods overseas, like Coca-Cola and Philip Morris, benefit because American products become cheaper and more competitive abroad. The domestic tourism industry may also gain as foreign travel gets more expensive for Americans, encouraging more vacation spending at home.

For the majority of U.S. businesses that don't export, a weak dollar raises the cost of imported materials and products, forcing price increases. Families feel the squeeze at grocery stores, gas stations, and airport currency exchanges, while businesses like medical supplier Gentell see shrinking margins.

Currency fluctuations are a normal part of a global economy. A weaker dollar can help correct trade imbalances by making exports rise and imports fall. However, the adjustment is rarely smooth; it often triggers inflation and can take years to produce the intended rebalancing, as past episodes like the Plaza Accord of 1985 illustrate.

If the dollar stays weak, pressure may grow on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to support it, which could slow the economy. International partners might protest, or the U.S. could push for a coordinated currency agreement. For young people, a sustained weak dollar could reshape the job market toward manufacturing and tourism but also make overseas study and travel more expensive for years.
